fixtures.basis: Arizona has no statewide code, so Mesa's adopted code sets the counts. Mesa adopts the 2024 International Plumbing Code; its amendment document (read in full) leaves the ratios of Table 403.1, Section 403.1.1 (half men, half women; fractions round up), Section 403.1.2 and Section 424.2 (urinals) as they are. It changes three things in Chapter 4: footnote e of Table 403.1 (no service sink for business and mercantile at 100 occupants or fewer), Exception 2 of Section 403.2 (separate rooms not required at 25 occupants or fewer, model: 15) and Section 410.2 (no drinking fountain at 50 occupants or fewer). The same three changes are repeated in the building code amendments (Table 2902.1, 2902.2, 2902.6). The city's own Plumbing Plan Submittal Checklist confirms the unamended urinal rule (67% assembly and educational, 50% others) and works a sample count from the unamended business ratio. The toilet counts therefore equal the model code's and the state pack's; only the separate-rooms threshold differs. The unamended table rows were read on UpCodes' copy of the 2024 IPC as adopted by New Hampshire (secondary; UpCodes has no Mesa copy and ICC's site blocks automated access).

amendment.text: Separate toilet rooms for each sex are not required in any structure or tenant space with a total occupant load of 25 or fewer (model code: 15 or fewer). The model code's other exceptions stay: mercantile at 100 or fewer, business at 25 or fewer. Service sinks are not required for business and mercantile uses at 100 occupants or fewer. The toilet ratios and the urinal substitution rule are not amended.

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Mesa job sites. Price your restroom, pick a material for the desert climate and see the rules that apply.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Mesa schools, medical offices, manufacturing plants and ballparks, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.fire_bullet: - **Fire safety:** Mesa's building rules require solid plastic (HDPE) partitions to pass a fire test. Ask for the fire-rated version.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** Mesa sets the number of toilets by how many people use the building, and caps how many of the men's toilets may be urinals. The table below shows what that means.
extra_rule_bullets: - **Mesa access rules:** Mesa's building rules apply two accessibility standards, the federal one and a national standard in its 2017 edition, and the one that gives more access applies. A restroom meant mainly for children aged 3 through 12 may be designed to the federal guidelines for children instead.
page.restroom_bullet: - **Single-user and all-gender restrooms:** under Mesa's plumbing rules a one-person restroom must be marked as open to everyone. A shared all-gender room may take the place of separate men's and women's rooms if every toilet sits in its own compartment with a door and every urinal has its own partitioned area. A measure Arizona voters approved in November 2026 says that from January 1, 2027, a school or athletic association may not authorize anyone to use a restroom, locker room or shower room that is part of its athletics facilities and is not designated for that person's sex.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Mesa issues tenant improvement permits for commercial interior work, with a faster on-site review for minor interior remodels. The city keeps its own list of work that needs no permit, and its commercial pages don't say whether replacing toilet partitions is on it. Ask Mesa Permit Services at 480-644-4273 whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.stalls_intro: Arizona has no statewide building rules, so Mesa's own rules decide. Mesa counts toilets by a building's capacity: the most people it is designed to hold at one time, worked out from its floor area. It isn't the number of staff or of visitors in a day. Half are counted as men and half as women. Every toilet needs a stall. Urinals are optional: in the men's room they may take the place of up to half of the toilets, or up to two thirds in restaurants and schools, so the table shows men's toilets as stalls.
page.stalls_after: These are minimums for the whole building, and at least one stall in each room must be wheelchair accessible. A shop designed for 100 people or fewer, and any other building or tenant space designed for 25 or fewer, doesn't need separate men's and women's rooms. Confirm the count with Mesa Development Services.
page.capacity: To find your building's capacity, Mesa's building rules count an office at one person per 150 square feet of floor, a restaurant dining room at one per 15 square feet and a classroom at one per 20. Your architect or Mesa Development Services sets the final number.
page.install_rule: On permitted commercial work Mesa asks for a Contractor Licensure Verification Form and an Arizona Registrar of Contractors license, and Development Services issues permits through its online portal, DIMES. Arizona requires a state Registrar of Contractors license for commercial installation work of $1,000 or more. Confirm what your project needs with Mesa Development Services. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: A contractor on a commercial job of $1,000 or more in Arizona needs a state Registrar of Contractors license.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** Arizona has no wage law for public jobs, and state law bars cities, counties and school districts from requiring prevailing wages in their contracts. On federally funded work the federal rate applies: $33.19 an hour plus $19.20 in benefits for a carpenter on building work in Maricopa County.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 8.3% in Mesa: 5.6% state, 0.7% Maricopa County and 2% city.
page.buyers_extra: - **Ballparks, sports complexes and recreation centers:** HDPE or phenolic in restrooms that take game-day crowds and are hosed down afterwards.

R10-3-404 under the Arizonans with Disabilities Act, A.R.S. 41-1492 et seq.); ICC A117.1-2017 (Mesa Building Code Section 1102.1); Mesa Building Code (Mesa City Code Title 4, Chapter 2, Ordinance No. 5980): 2024 International Building Code with Mesa amendments; Mesa Plumbing Code (Title 4, Chapter 5, Ordinance No. 5983): 2024 International Plumbing Code with Mesa amendments; both in force for permit applications since January 8, 2026; Mesa Administrative Code (Title 4, Chapter 1, Section 4-1-4 for permits and work exempt from permits); NFPA 286 for HDPE (International Building Code Section 803.9).
